name: Blue
lede: Blue is the color of a clear sky and deep water: a hue the ancient world barely named, the Middle Ages raised to heaven, and the modern West has picked as its favorite color for more than a century.

sections.title: A color without a word
sections.body:
Blue is the color of a clear sky and of deep water, yet for much of history it barely had a name. Latin had no firm basic word for it, only vague terms such as *caeruleus* and *glaucus*, and the Romance languages later borrowed two foreign words: Germanic *blau* and *azure*, from the Persian name of the stone lapis lazuli [1][4]. In Homer's poems the Greek *kyaneos* could describe a bright iris or a black mourning robe, but never the sky or the sea [1]. When Gladstone counted Homer's color words in 1858, black came up about 170 times and blue not once; Lazarus Geiger found that the Vedic hymns never call the sky blue either [2].

From such counts, nineteenth-century scholars concluded that the Greeks could not see blue [1][3]. That idea is wrong, and long abandoned. Their eyes were the same as ours; what differed was vocabulary and value, and Pastoureau points out that Corneille and La Fontaine never use the word either, though their readers saw blue perfectly well [1][3].

The word stayed slippery. Old French *bloi*, the source of English *blue*, could mean blue or yellow [4]. Welsh *glas* runs from green to blue, Japanese *ao* can mean green, blue or dark, and Vietnamese and Korean do not split green from blue [5][6]. Russian has two basic blues, *siniy* for dark and *goluboy* for light, and Eckstut reports that Russians take a moment longer to name a blue that sits between them [6][7]. In Berlin and Kay's contested sequence of color words, blue arrives only after red, yellow and green [9]. In Latin Christian writing up to the ninth century, blue makes up under 1 per cent of color words [8].

sections.title: Stones, glass and the first synthetic pigment
sections.body:
Blue's first great invention was Egyptian [10]. From about 2500 BC Egyptian craftsmen fired lime, copper and quartz together at 800 to 900°C to make [[egyptian-blue|Egyptian blue]], the oldest synthetic pigment [10]. They called it artificial lapis lazuli, and for them blue meant the sky, the Nile and creation; the god Amun-Ra had blue skin [11]. The pigment spread across the Mediterranean, and pots of it sat unused in Pompeii's color shops [10]. That is one reason Gage reads Pliny's story of Greek painters working with only four colors as a moral preference, not a fact of the workshop [12].

The costliest blue came from a stone. Through the Middle Ages almost all [[lapis-lazuli|lapis lazuli]] came from Badakhshan in Afghanistan, and Marco Polo visited the mines in 1271 [4]. The glittering specks in it are not gold, as medieval writers hoped, but iron pyrite [1][13]. Grinding lapis gives only a greyish powder; the method of extracting pure blue, kneading the powder into a dough of wax and resin and washing the blue out, seems to be a medieval invention, and good ultramarine appears in Western painting around 1200 [4]. Cennini priced the best at eight ducats an ounce, and in 1521 Dürer paid about a hundred times the cost of an earth pigment for it [4].

Most painters used azurite, a copper mineral, which was the commonest blue of antiquity and the Middle Ages [1]. It is unstable. Over the years it can turn into green malachite, which is why many Italian church blues are now green, and under old varnish thick azurite darkens almost to black [14]. Glass behaved better. The blue windows of Saint-Denis and Chartres, made in the mid-twelfth century, were colored with cobalt and have barely changed [1]. The so-called lost blue of Chartres is a myth: the recipe survives, and only the old furnaces and impure materials cannot be reproduced [15].

sections.title: Woad and indigo
sections.body:
For cloth, blue meant one molecule from many plants. European woad and tropical indigo give exactly the same blue, though woad leaves hold far less of it, and no specialist can tell from the blue which plant it came from [16][47]. The dye does not need a mordant: cloth comes out of the vat yellow-green and turns blue in the air within minutes [17][18]. The Romans knew indigo came from India but took it for a stone, because it arrived as hard cakes [1].

Woad made medieval fortunes. From the 1230s it was produced almost industrially, and Toulouse and Erfurt grew rich on what Pastoureau calls blue gold [18]. Then indigo arrived in quantity, and Europe tried to keep it out [19]. French edicts of 1609, 1624 and 1642 made dyeing with indigo a capital offense, the emperor Ferdinand III called it the devil's color in 1654, and it was legalized in France and Germany only in 1737 [19][20]. Woad growers spread the claim that indigo was corrosive; it was not, since the two dyes are the same chemical [21].

The laboratory ended the plantations. India had 2,800 indigo factories in 1870 [21]. Adolf von Baeyer synthesized indigo in 1877 or 1878, depending on the book, BASF was selling it by 1897, and by the First World War most of Europe's natural indigo market had gone [21][19]. Denim then saved the dye. Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis made riveted indigo work trousers from 1873, and jeans stayed ordinary workwear until the late 1960s, not rebel clothing [22][19]. Where the word *denim* comes from is debated: *serge de Nîmes* is a guess, not a fact [19]. The dyers' own shade names survive in English: the eighteenth-century scale of indigo blues ran from milk and pearl through queen's blue to [[navy|navy blue]], and gave us [[royal-blue|royal blue]] as well [23]. More on the dye is in [[indigo]].

sections.title: From barbarian color to heaven
sections.body:
To the Romans blue was a barbarian color [1]. Caesar and Tacitus describe Celts and Germans painting their bodies blue, and Roman comedy mocked blue eyes [1]. Whether the Britons' paint was woad is uncertain, since Caesar's word *vitrum* may mean something else [24][20]. Carolingian nobles kept blue out of court, and until the twelfth century it was mainly a peasant color [1]. Early medieval treatises on color symbolism never mention it, and the Church's liturgical colors still have no place for it [1].

Then, in about a century, blue went to heaven. Abbot Suger made it the color of divine light in the windows of Saint-Denis in the 1130s and 1140s, the Virgin's robe became bright blue in the twelfth century, and the kings of France took a blue shield with gold lilies [1][18]. Between 1230 and 1250, Saint Louis and Henry III of England both began to wear it [18]. Heraldry measures the change: blue appears in about 5 per cent of coats of arms around 1200, 25 per cent around 1300 and 30 per cent by 1400 [18]. [[madder|Madder]] merchants, losing trade to woad, paid to have devils painted blue in church windows; it did not work [25][18].

The Virgin's blue had a price as well as a meaning [4]. Contracts specified ultramarine by cost: Andrea del Sarto's *Madonna of the Harpies* of 1515 had to use blue at five florins the ounce [4][26]. Gage warns that a canonical blue Virgin is overstated: Byzantine art often dressed her in purple, and van Eyck often in red [26]. When Pope Julius II wanted the Sistine ceiling retouched with ultramarine and gold, Michelangelo answered that the men painted there were poor and wore no gold [27].

Blue kept rising. In Florence's clothing inventory of 1343 to 1345 it appears in only 19 per cent of garments, against 67 per cent for red [28]. Four centuries later, Hellot's 1750 dyeing treatise gave 192 pages to blue and 155 to red [29]. In medieval thought blue was a warm color, sometimes the warmest, and it became fully cool only in the nineteenth century [30][48].

sections.title: The favorite color
sections.body:
The eighteenth century belonged to blue. [[prussian-blue|Prussian blue]], made by accident in Berlin between about 1704 and 1707, cost about a tenth of ultramarine, and despite its chemistry it does not release cyanide [4][19]. Light blue, long dismissed as faded peasant cloth, became court fashion, and after Goethe's *Werther* (1774) young men across Europe copied the hero's blue coat [19]. In 1790 revolutionary France declared the blue of the French Guards its national blue, and in the nineteenth century French blue drifted politically from republicans to moderates and the right [19].

Between about 1910 and 1950 uniforms for police, postmen and sailors moved from black to navy, and from the 1930s civilian men followed in navy blazers and suits [19]. Since the late nineteenth century, polls in Western Europe and the United States have found more than half of people naming blue as their favorite color [19]. Pastoureau warns that such polls are quick and shallow, and suggests blue wins because it offends no one [19]. The League of Nations, the United Nations and the European Union all chose it as the neutral color [30].

New blues kept coming. Louis-Jacques Thénard made cobalt blue around 1802, at a minister's request for a cheaper substitute for ultramarine [31][49]. In 1824 a French society offered 6,000 francs for an artificial ultramarine; Jean-Baptiste Guimet won in 1828, though Christian Gmelin disputed his priority, and the synthetic sold at a hundredth or less of the natural stone's price [4]. Cerulean blue followed in the 1860s [31], and a phthalocyanine blue noticed by accident in 1928 became the ideal cyan of color printing [21][4]. Yves Klein patented his International Klein Blue in 1960, an ultramarine in a resin binder that keeps the powder's velvet [4]. Practical blue LEDs arrived only around 1990, and their inventors shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics [32].

Some blues did not last. Prussian blue fades in light when mixed with much white, which washed out skies by Gainsborough, Watteau and Canaletto, and smalt, a ground cobalt glass, has browned Velázquez's sky in his *Immaculate Conception* [14]. In old tapestries the fugitive yellow laid over blue to make green has faded first, so the leaves have turned blue; the only color in the Bayeux Tapestry still as it was is its woad blue [33].

sections.title: Why the sky is blue, and why blue looks dark
sections.body:
The sky is blue because air scatters short wavelengths of sunlight far more than long ones [34]. Tyndall blamed dust for it, and Einstein showed that air molecules alone are enough [15]. At sunset light crosses so much air that the blue is scattered away, leaving reds and yellows [34]. The same air turns distance blue: Leonardo told painters that a wall five times farther away should be painted five times bluer [35]. Shadows on a clear day are bluish because the sky lights them, and with distance dark things lighten and turn blue first [36][37].

Blue is rare in living things. No vertebrate makes a blue pigment; the blue of a peacock's feather or a butterfly's wing is structure, which is why it shifts as you tilt your head [38]. Blue human eyes work the same way: little melanin, and a structure that scatters blue light [39]. Gems are different. A sapphire is blue because traces of iron and titanium sit in corundum, the same mineral that chromium turns into ruby [43].

The eye treats blue as dark. In daylight, blue light at 450 nanometres gives about a twentieth of the brightness response of the same amount of green light [40]. Munsell found that blue reaches its strongest chroma only when it is very dark, the opposite of yellow [41]. At dusk the balance flips: as the rods take over, a given amount of blue looks about a hundred times brighter than the same amount of red [40]. Moonlit scenes look blue because of how the eye works in dim light, not because moonlight is blue: it is reflected sunlight, measured as slightly redder than direct sun [42].

sections.title: Blue in painting
sections.body:
Blue was the hardest color for fresco. Azurite turns green when wet and indigo blackens, so ultramarine was needed, and Giotto's blue ceiling in the Arena Chapel, of about 1305, is the great exception [4]. Ultramarine also looks weaker in oil than in egg tempera, so Renaissance painters mixed it with lead white, which opened a range of paler blues [4]. Raphael softened the Virgin's ultramarine with white in *[[art:nga-26|The Alba Madonna]]* [44]. Vermeer saved money by using lapis only in the top layers, over underpainting in azurite, smalt or indigo [45].

Varnish can hide blue entirely. Before its cleaning in 1967 and 1968, Titian's *Bacchus and Ariadne* in London had a muddy brownish sky; under the old varnish was a radiant azurite blue, and the cleaned picture caused an outcry [14]. Monet painted snow in shadow as blue because skylight alone lights it [46]. Picasso's blue-period pictures still read well in black and white, Livingstone notes, because lightness carries the form and the blue carries the mood [40].

Leonardo claimed that blue and yellow light combine into a beautiful green. Ball points out that he never did the experiment: mixed as light, they make white [44].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of this page's blue covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 9 works, and none is older than 1655 [80]. The earliest is Samuel Cooper's portrait miniature of Lady Clarke, and the one where it covers most is Martín Rico's view of the Alhambra from 1871, at 16 per cent [80]. Widen the net to any clearly colored blue (CIELAB chroma of 30 or more over five per cent of the canvas) and it turns up in 94 paintings, against 2,044 for red by the same rule [80]. Lower the bar to chroma 15 and blue reaches 862 paintings; its rate in our twentieth-century works, 11 per cent, is five times that of our seventeenth-century ones [80].

Part of that is history, since vivid blue was dear before 1828 [4]. Part is the photographs: these are aged, varnished paintings, and old varnish pushes blue toward grey, green or brown [80][14]. Look at the largest color of *The Alba Madonna* as photographed: a greyed blue, not ultramarine [80]. In Gainsborough's *[[art:commons-Q3700536|Portrait of a Lady in Blue]]*, the only bluish color among the six largest is a grey-teal [80]. A color match is not a pigment test [80].

The swatch is a choice too. The CSS keyword `blue` is the far more violet #0000FF, the American color standard calls this region vivid blue, and our nearest named neighbors include [[commelina-blue|Commelina Blue]], [[royal-blue|Royal blue]] and [[lapis-lazuli|Lapis Lazuli]] [81]. In Google Books the word *blue* stands at half its peak in 1800 and climbs to its highest point in 2016 [82].

questions.q: Why do the leaves in many old tapestries look blue today?
choices: The yellow dyed over the blue to make green has faded, leaving the blue
Medieval weavers believed leaves were blue
Indigo darkens and spreads over time
Museum lighting turns green to blue
questions.answer: The yellow dyed over the blue to make green has faded, leaving the blue

questions.q: True or false: the glittering specks in lapis lazuli are real gold.
Why does a clear sky look blue?
choices: Air molecules scatter short, blue wavelengths of sunlight more than long ones
The sky reflects the color of the oceans
Dust in the upper air is blue
questions.answer: Air molecules scatter short, blue wavelengths of sunlight more than long ones

openers: Homer never once calls the sea or the sky blue.
Look at the leaves in an old tapestry: many are blue now, because the yellow laid over the blue has faded.
In 1515 a contract fixed the price of the Virgin's blue: five florins the ounce.
